title: Why a camel has a hump, a woodpecker a hard head and an octopus no bones

summary.text: A camel can cross the Thar for days with almost nothing to drink, yet the hump on her back holds no water at all. It holds fat. Your child melts ice under cloth to find out why the fat sits in one lump and not all over her body. Then they test why a camel's wide foot does not sink, and meet a woodpecker whose head takes thousands of hard knocks a day, and an octopus with three hearts and no bones. Every odd body part turns out to be an answer to a problem, and every answer has a price.
summary.art: A camel standing on a dune at sunset, a woodpecker clinging to a trunk and an octopus on a reef, each with a small glowing circle around the body part that looks odd.

intro.hook: A camel can walk for days across the Thar desert without a drink. On her back she carries a big hump. Most people say the hump is full of water. Is that true?
intro.text: Before you read on, guess what is inside the hump. Is it water, fat, muscle or air? Say your guess and the reason for it. Now think of two more animals with a part that looks odd. A woodpecker has a pointed beak and bangs it on wood all day. An octopus has soft arms and no bones. Each odd part is a clue to a problem that animal has to solve to stay alive. In this unit you find the problems, test two of them with ice and dough, and discover that every answer has a price.
intro.art: A child looking at three cards on a table: a camel's hump, a woodpecker's beak and an octopus's arm, with a question mark above each.

outcomes: I can explain that an odd body part is an answer to a problem in the animal's way of life, and name the problem and one price for the camel's hump, the woodpecker's head and the octopus's soft body.
I can run a fair test to show that the same amount of insulation works differently when it is spread out or lumped in one place, and say what that means for a camel's fat.
I can show that the same weight sinks less on a wider foot, and explain how a camel's foot, a snowshoe and a softer tyre do the same job.
I can say how a woodpecker climbs, eats and hits wood, and describe what scientists still argue about in her head.
I can say how an octopus moves, breathes and squeezes through gaps, and name a price of her soft body.
I can explain a surprising result in three parts: what I think (claim), what I saw (evidence) and why (reasoning).
I can explain why an animal does not grow a part because she needs it, and how chance differences and survival shape bodies over many generations.
I can give an example of two animals that solved the same problem in different ways.

terms.meaning: A feature of a body that helps an animal live in the place and the way she lives. It builds up over many generations, not in one life.
terms.example: A camel's wide foot pads are an adaptation to walking on loose sand.
terms.art: A camel's foot print on sand next to a thin horse hoof print that has sunk deeper.

terms.meaning: A deal where a body part gives a gain and also costs something. A feature that is good in one life is often poor in another.
terms.example: A camel's wide foot floats on sand, but it slips on wet clay.
terms.art: A balance scale with a gain on one side and a cost on the other.

terms.meaning: Fat the body keeps as a supply of energy for later. Fat holds about twice as much energy as the same weight of sugar or starch.
terms.example: A camel's hump is a store of fat.
terms.art: A camel's hump drawn as a cutaway full of pale fat.

terms.meaning: Anything that slows heat as it travels in or out. Cloth, fur, feathers and fat are all insulation.
terms.example: A woollen shawl slows the heat leaving your body.
terms.art: A child wrapped in a shawl with arrows of heat shown slowed at the cloth.

terms.meaning: How hard a weight pushes on each small patch of the ground it stands on. The same weight on a small patch gives a big pressure, and on a big patch gives a small one.
terms.example: A girl standing on one toe presses the floor harder than when she stands on her whole foot.
terms.art: A weight pressing on a small foot and on a wide foot, with the small foot sunk deeper in sand.

terms.meaning: A thick, springy cushion under the foot. A camel's pad is broad, and it spreads out when she puts her weight on it.
terms.example: The leathery pad under a camel's toes.
terms.art: The underside of a camel's foot showing a wide pad with two toes.

terms.meaning: Feet with two toes pointing forward and two pointing back. This grip is good for clinging to a trunk.
terms.art: A woodpecker's foot gripping bark, with two toes forward and two back.

terms.meaning: The small bone system that holds up the tongue. In many woodpeckers it is long and curls around the back of the skull.
terms.example: A woodpecker's tongue is rooted at the back of her head and curls around her skull.
terms.art: A woodpecker's skull drawn with a long tongue curled around the back and out through the beak.

terms.meaning: The muscular bag of an octopus's body that holds her organs and gills. It fills with water and squeezes it out.
terms.example: An octopus breathes by moving water through her mantle.
terms.art: An octopus with the mantle drawn as a cutaway showing the gills and a funnel.

terms.meaning: Moving forward by pushing a stream of fluid backwards. The fluid pushes back on the body with an equal force.
terms.example: An octopus squirts water out of a funnel and shoots away.
terms.art: An octopus with an arrow showing water squirting backwards and the body shooting forwards.

terms.meaning: A copper-based chemical that carries oxygen in the blood of an octopus. It makes the blood blue.
terms.example: Octopus blood is blue because of haemocyanin.
terms.art: A drop of blue blood beside a drop of red blood, labelled copper and iron.

terms.meaning: A tiny stretchy sac of colour in the skin of an octopus. Muscles open it wide or squeeze it small, so the colour of the skin can change in a moment.
terms.example: An octopus turns brown, then white, as her chromatophores open and close.
terms.art: A zoomed-in patch of octopus skin with small colour sacs, some open and some squeezed.

terms.meaning: The small differences between animals of the same kind. No two are exactly alike.
terms.example: Some camel calves have slightly wider feet than others.
terms.art: A row of five camel feet, each a slightly different width.

terms.meaning: When animals with a helpful difference survive and have more young than others, so that the difference becomes common over many generations.
terms.example: Calves with broader pads walked farther on sand, lived longer and left more young.
terms.art: A family tree of camels where the feet get slightly wider down the generations.

terms.meaning: When two kinds of animals that are not close relatives end up with a similar body part because they faced a similar problem.
terms.example: Octopuses and humans both have eyes with a lens, but their eyes grew separately.
terms.art: An octopus eye and a human eye side by side, each with a lens, joined by an arrow labelled separate paths.

terms.meaning: Colour or shape that makes an animal hard to see against her background.
terms.example: An octopus on a reef turns the colour and pattern of the rock beside her.
terms.art: An octopus almost invisible against a coral rock.

explanations.concept: Every odd body part answers a problem
explanations.definition: An adaptation is a feature of a body that helps an animal survive and have young in the place and the way she lives.
explanations.description: An animal has to solve the same few problems every day. She must get food, get water, get oxygen, move around, stay at the right temperature and stay safe. Each place sets these problems in a different way. A dune is hot and soft and short of water. A tree trunk is straight and hard, and food hides inside it. A reef has many cracks and many hungry fish. So the body parts of animals in these places are different. The way to understand an odd part is to ask three questions. What problem does it solve? How does it solve it? What does it cost? We use these three questions all through this unit. Humans are animals too. Our feet, hands and backbone are answers as well, and they also have prices.
examples: A camel's hump keeps fat for lean times.
A woodpecker's stiff tail props her against a trunk.
An octopus's soft body squeezes into a crack to hide.
explanations.art: Three cards in a row: problem, part and price, with a camel's hump drawn on them.
explanations.context: This is the big idea of the unit. We will use it for each animal in turn.

explanations.concept: The camel's hump holds fat, not water
explanations.definition: A camel's hump is a lump of fat under the skin. The camel uses the fat as a store of energy when food is hard to find.
explanations.description: The hump of a big dromedary camel can hold up to about 30 kilograms of fat. When the camel finds little to eat, her body slowly uses the fat, and the hump shrinks and flops to one side. When she eats well again, the hump fills out. Fat is a good store because it holds about twice as much energy as the same weight of sugar. Why is it all in one lump? Fat is also a blanket, and a thick blanket all over would trap the heat inside her body. By keeping the fat on her back, the camel leaves the rest of her skin thin, so the heat can leave. The lump on top may also shade her back from the Sun. Burning fat does make a little water, but it also needs more breathing, and breathing loses water. So the hump is a food store, not a water tank.
examples: The Ice Test in this unit: the same cloth keeps ice cold when it is spread all over, but not when it is in one lump.
A thin, hungry camel has a small hump that flops. A well-fed camel has a firm, tall hump.
A Bactrian camel, from the cold deserts of Central Asia, has two humps and a thick winter coat.
explanations.art: A camel cut through the middle to show fat in the hump and thin skin along the sides, with arrows of heat leaving the sides.
explanations.context: This explains the Ice Test. It says what the hump holds and why the fat is in one lump.

explanations.definition: Water saving is any way a body loses less water or takes in more, so that the animal can go longer between drinks.
explanations.description: A camel is not good at finding water. She is good at keeping it. First, her body temperature goes up by day and down by night. In one study, a camel with no water let her temperature rise from about 34 to about 41 degrees Celsius. A body that is allowed to get hot does not need to sweat as much to stay cool. Second, the inside of her nose is damp and cool. As she breathes out, it catches water from the air, and she breathes it back in. Third, her dung is dry and her wee is thick. Fourth, her red blood cells are oval, not round, and they can swell a great deal without bursting when she drinks. A very thirsty camel can drink about 100 litres or more in a few minutes. She can lose about a quarter of her body weight in water and live. A person is in danger long before that.
examples: A dehydrated camel's temperature can swing by 6 or 7 degrees in a day.
A camel's long double eyelashes and closing nostrils keep sand out.
A person drinks about 2 litres a day, and a very thirsty camel can drink about 50 times as much at one go.
explanations.art: A camel with labels: damp nose catches water from breath, temperature goes up by day, oval blood cells.
explanations.context: This is the second part of the camel story. It shows the camel's other ways of keeping water.

explanations.concept: A wide foot floats on soft ground
explanations.definition: Pressure is the push of a weight on each small patch of the surface it stands on. Pressure equals the weight divided by the area.
explanations.description: A big camel can weigh 600 kilograms, and a sharp hoof would sink in sand like a nail. A camel's foot is a broad, soft pad that spreads out as she puts her weight down. The same weight is shared over a bigger patch, so each small patch is pushed less, and the sand holds. This is why a person in snowshoes walks on snow, and why a tractor tyre with some air let out grips a muddy field. In the Foot Test, doubling the width of the foot makes the area 4 times as big, so the pressure becomes 4 times smaller. It is a fair trade only on soft ground. On wet clay, the broad pad slides, and a camel can slip and fall. The Kharai camels of Kutch wade and swim out to islands to eat mangrove leaves. Their wide feet help them in soft mud.
examples: Camel feet, snowshoes, a duck's webbed feet and a wide tractor tyre all spread weight.
A high-heeled shoe presses the floor much harder than a flat sandal on the same person.
In the Foot Test, a tumbler on a bottle cap sinks into dough, and the same tumbler on a plate hardly does.
explanations.art: Two feet on sand: a narrow hoof sunk deep and a wide camel pad on the surface, with small arrows for pressure.
explanations.context: This explains the Foot Test. It says why a wide foot does not sink.

explanations.concept: How a woodpecker climbs, eats and hits wood
explanations.definition: A woodpecker is a bird whose body is built for climbing trunks and getting food from wood.
explanations.description: A woodpecker has four problems. First, she has to cling to a straight trunk. Most woodpeckers have two toes forward and two back, with sharp claws. Their tail feathers are stiff, and the woodpecker leans on them as a third foot. Second, she has to open the wood. Her beak is like a chisel, and her neck muscles are strong. She can hit up to about 20 times a second, in short bursts. Third, she has to reach the insects deep in the wood. Her tongue is long and sticky, with a barbed tip. In some woodpeckers it reaches as much as 10 centimetres past the beak. The tongue is anchored at the back of her head, and it curls around her skull. Fourth, she has to do this without hurting her brain.
examples: The Black-rumped Flameback, a woodpecker you can see in city parks in India, taps on tree trunks.
A woodpecker's tongue is rooted far back and curls around the skull, so it can reach very far.
Her stiff tail props her up like the third leg of a stool.
explanations.art: A woodpecker on a trunk showing the toes, the stiff tail used as a prop, the chisel beak, and the tongue curled around the skull.
explanations.context: This shows how a woodpecker climbs, eats and hits wood. The next card asks how her head survives.

explanations.concept: How does a woodpecker's head survive the hits?
explanations.description: A woodpecker's head stops very suddenly each time it hits the wood. A hit like this would badly hurt a person's brain. For years, books said that woodpeckers have a built-in shock absorber, like a helmet. Scientists are no longer sure. The ideas below are all being studied, and they may be partly true together.
examples: Her skull and beak are strong, and her brain is small and sits snugly in the skull.
She hits in a straight line, so her head does not twist, and twisting is what harms brains most.
Some researchers think she braces her neck muscles at the moment of the hit, and closes a thin eyelid to protect her eye.

perspectives.who: The shock-absorber idea (older books, and a study of 2011)
perspectives.explanation: Soft, spongy bone and the long tongue bone around the skull take the knock, and spread it over the head, so the brain is spared.
High-speed videos showed that the head works like a stiff hammer. It sends almost all of its energy into the wood, and takes little of it into the skull. The cushion matters less than we thought.
A tiny brain has very little weight, so the force on it in each hit is small. A larger animal with the same hits would be hurt.

explanations.art: Three small drawings of a woodpecker's head: a spongy cushion, a stiff hammer, and a tiny brain in a snug skull.
explanations.context: This is a question that scientists have not settled. Here are the main ideas.

explanations.concept: How an octopus moves, breathes and squeezes
explanations.definition: An octopus is a soft-bodied sea animal with eight arms, three hearts and no bones. Her only big hard part is her beak.
explanations.description: An octopus has no skeleton, so she can pour herself through any gap that is wider than her beak. She uses this to hide in cracks and to open shells and jars. She has two ways to move. Most of the time she crawls over the sea floor on her arms, which is slow and cheap. When she is in danger, she fills her mantle with water and squeezes it out through a funnel. The water jets backwards, and she shoots away. The same mantle space holds her gills and she breathes through it. Her blood is blue, because it carries oxygen with copper instead of iron. Two of her three hearts push blood through the gills, and the third pushes it round the body. Her arms are lined with suckers that can taste what they touch.
examples: A common octopus can squeeze through a hole not much bigger than her beak.
In the Squeeze Test in this unit, a soft dough ball passes through a small hole, and a hard ball of the same size cannot.
An octopus drilling a shell, and then eating the soft animal inside.
explanations.art: An octopus cutaway showing the mantle, funnel, gills, three hearts and the beak between the arms.
explanations.context: This shows how an octopus moves, breathes and squeezes. The next card asks what it costs her.

explanations.definition: A trade-off is a deal in which getting one gain means paying a cost somewhere else.
explanations.description: A camel's wide pad floats on sand, but she slips on wet clay. Her hump is a store of food, but it is heavy to carry, and it flops when food is short. An octopus has no bones, so she can squeeze into a crack, but swimming tires her quickly. While she swims by jet, the heart that pumps blood to her body slows or stops, so she must rest. Her blue blood carries less oxygen than red blood does, which is a price she pays in warm water. A woodpecker's head is built for hitting, but she can live only where there are trees with wood to open. Humans have trade-offs too. Walking upright frees our hands, and many of us get backache. So no body is the best at everything. A body is good for one way of life.
examples: The same fat is a good coat in a cold sea and a trap for heat in a desert.
An octopus squeezes through a crack but cannot run or swim far.
A human's upright back frees the hands, and often aches.
explanations.art: Three animals on a balance: a camel, a woodpecker and an octopus, each with a gain on one side and a cost on the other.
explanations.context: This is the idea that ties the three animals together. Each gain has a cost.

explanations.definition: Convergent evolution is when two kinds of animals that are not close relatives end up with a similar body part, because they met a similar problem.
explanations.description: Octopuses and humans both have eyes with a round lens that makes a sharp picture. Our last shared ancestor lived more than 500 million years ago and had no such eyes. So the two eyes grew separately. They are not the same. In our eye, the nerve fibres run in front of the light-sensing cells, and make a blind spot where they leave the eye. In an octopus's eye, the nerve fibres run behind, so there is no blind spot. Bats and birds both fly with wings, but a bat's wing is a hand with long fingers, and a bird's wing is a row of feathers. The problem was the same, and the answers are different, because each started from a different body.
examples: Eyes of an octopus and of a human.
Wings of a bird and a bat.
Long, sticky tongues for catching insects in woodpeckers and in anteaters, who are not close relatives.
explanations.art: An octopus eye and a human eye drawn side by side, with the nerve fibres in front for ours and behind for the octopus.
explanations.context: This shows that two animals can meet the same problem and find different answers.

explanations.concept: How a body part comes to exist
explanations.definition: Natural selection is the way that helpful differences become common. Animals with a helpful difference survive and have more young, and the young inherit it.
explanations.description: An animal does not grow a hump or a wide foot because she needs one. A camel that stretches her feet all her life does not pass wider feet to her calves. What happens is slower. In every generation, young animals differ a little. Some calves have slightly wider pads. On soft sand, those calves walk farther, find more food and live longer. They have more calves, and their calves inherit the wider pads. After thousands of generations, wide pads are normal. The camel family began in North America, tens of millions of years ago, and spread across the world. No one planned the hump. It is the result of many small differences that survived. This is also why bodies are never perfect. They are made from what was already there.
examples: Calves with slightly broader pads walk better on sand, so they leave more calves.
A giraffe stretching her neck in her own lifetime does not make her calves' necks longer.
Octopuses came from shelled ancestors, and lost the shell over a very long time.
explanations.art: Four generations of camels with feet getting slightly wider, with the one with the narrowest feet sinking in sand.
explanations.context: This says how a body part comes to exist. It also says what 'adapted' means.

agreed.text: A camel's hump is made of fat, and it does not hold water.
agreed.evidence: In the 1950s, Knut Schmidt-Nielsen and his team weighed camels in the Sahara as they went without water. The weight lost was water from the whole body, and the camels got it all back in one long drink. The hump itself is fat.

agreed.text: A camel can let her body temperature rise and fall by several degrees, and so use less water for sweating.
agreed.evidence: In the Sahara in 1956, scientists took the temperature of camels every day. Camels with no water had a much wider daily swing than camels that were given water.

agreed.text: An octopus has three hearts and blue blood.
agreed.evidence: Dissections and blood tests show two gill hearts and one body heart. The blue colour comes from copper in the chemical haemocyanin.

agreed.text: An octopus has about 500 million nerve cells, and about two thirds of them are in the arms.
agreed.evidence: Counts of nerve cells in the common octopus were made by researchers, and a famous review of 2012 reports them.

agreed.text: Animals with similar problems can end up with similar parts that grew separately.
agreed.evidence: The genes and the early growth of octopus eyes and human eyes are different, even though the finished eyes look alike.

agreed.text: Wider feet press softer on the ground, because pressure is weight divided by area.
agreed.evidence: This is measured in physics laboratories and shown in the Foot Test.

challenging.claim: A camel's hump is a tank of water.
challenging.who: Many people, and many old books.
challenging.for: Camels go for days without a drink, and the hump is the biggest thing on a camel that looks like a store.
challenging.against: When the hump is cut open, it is fat. A camel that has gone without water shrinks all over, and the hump does not hold the water she lacks.
challenging.context: This is a very common idea about camels. Here is what the evidence says.

challenging.claim: A woodpecker has a built-in shock absorber in her head.
challenging.who: Many books and websites, and some studies.
challenging.for: A woodpecker's skull has spongy bone, and her tongue bone curls around it. A study of 2011 argued that these take part of the knock.
challenging.against: A study of 2022 used high-speed video of living woodpeckers and found that the head works like a stiff hammer. It said very little of the knock is soaked up by the skull.
challenging.context: This is an idea about how a woodpecker's head survives. Scientists have not agreed.

challenging.for: The word tentacle is often used for any long, soft limb.
challenging.against: Scientists call an octopus's limbs arms, because they carry suckers along their whole length. A squid has eight arms and two longer tentacles that have suckers only at the tip.
challenging.context: This is about the right word for an octopus's limbs. The word matters because the shapes are different.

challenging.claim: An octopus cannot match colours, because her eyes cannot see colour.
challenging.who: Some scientists, because octopus eyes have only one kind of light-sensing cell.
challenging.for: With one kind of light-sensing cell, an octopus should not see colours as we do.
challenging.against: Octopuses match the colours of rocks and weed very well. Some scientists think the skin itself senses light. Others think her oddly shaped pupil lets her work out colours from how the light blurs. Neither idea has been settled.
challenging.context: This is a puzzle about how a camouflaging octopus does so well. Nobody knows yet.

challenging.claim: An animal grows a new body part because she needs it.
challenging.who: Many people, and a very old idea.
challenging.for: It seems natural. Giraffes need to reach, and they have long necks.
challenging.against: A giraffe who stretches her neck does not pass a longer neck to her calves. Small differences already exist, and the animals with helpful ones live and have more young. Needing a part does not make the part appear.
challenging.context: This is an old idea about how bodies change. Here is why scientists no longer hold it.

challenging.claim: An octopus's arms think for themselves, like eight small brains.
challenging.for: A cut-off arm still reaches for food and pulls it toward its mouth. Most of an octopus's nerve cells are in her arms.
challenging.against: The arms are linked to the central brain, which sends them general orders. Many scientists say each arm acts on local reflexes, and they do not call that thinking.
challenging.context: This is a question about how much of an octopus's thinking happens in her arms.

big_questions.q: A bee sees a flower as ultraviolet patterns, and a child sees it yellow. When an octopus touches a stone, her arm tastes it. Is it the same stone for her as for you?
big_questions.hint: Think about what each body can sense and what it cannot. Is the stone the same, or only the word 'stone'?

big_questions.q: If a body is a set of trade-offs, can any animal be called the best?
big_questions.hint: Best at what, and where? Think of the camel on wet clay and the octopus on dry land.

big_questions.q: Nobody planned a camel. How is it that her body fits her life so well?
big_questions.hint: Think about the many calves that did not do well, and what they did not pass on.

big_questions.q: Is a body made to fit a place, or is a place made to fit a body? Is a foot the shape of sand?
big_questions.hint: A foot and the ground it walks on fit each other like a key and a lock. Which one came first?

big_questions.q: If an octopus's arm can still reach for food after it is cut off, who is doing the reaching?
big_questions.hint: Think about the difference between a reflex, a decision and a feeling. Where might one end and the next begin?

big_questions.q: Humans are animals too. What are the trade-offs in a human body?
big_questions.hint: Look at your feet, your back, your hands and your big head. What did each give, and what did it cost?

big_questions.q: Is an animal with a simple body a 'simple' animal?
big_questions.hint: An octopus has no bones. Is she simple or complicated? What does 'simple' even mean?

big_questions.q: If you could add one body part to yourself, what would it cost you?
big_questions.hint: Think about a hump, a wide pad or a beak. What would you have to carry, eat or give up?

story.title: The Jeep and the Camel's Foot
story.note: A made-up story. The science in it is real. Letting some air out of tyres on soft sand makes the tyre flatter, so the same weight is spread over a bigger patch and the vehicle sinks less. A camel's wide pad does the same job, and camels do slip on wet clay. Always pump the tyres up again before driving on a hard road.
text: Dr. Revathi had come from Chennai to Bikaner for a month's work with camel doctors. Now she had driven three hours into the Thar. A camel calf at a small dhani had stopped drinking. The vaccine in her cool box would not last in the heat, and the jeep was already late.
Then the road ended. Ahead lay a long slope of pale sand, rippled like the skin of milk. 'Hold on,' said Karim, the driver, and he pressed the pedal.

The jeep roared up the slope. Halfway, the back wheels began to spin. Sand flew out in two brown fans, and the jeep sank slowly to its belly. Karim pressed the pedal harder. The wheels dug two deep pits, and the jeep sank even more.
'Stop,' said Revathi. 'You are digging us in deeper.' Karim switched off the engine. The silence of the desert came in, and a small bell rang somewhere in it.
Over the dune came a camel with a girl on her back. The girl was about nine. Her name was Gauri, and the calf was her grandfather's. She had walked out to look for the doctor.

The camel was a big female called Bhuri. She stepped down the slope, and Revathi noticed something. Bhuri was heavy, as heavy as the jeep's engine. But she did not sink. Her feet left shallow, round marks, as if someone had pressed saucers into the sand.
Karim got out and dug at the wheels with a plate from the cool box. Gauri slid down and watched him for a while. Then she looked at the jeep's tyre, and at Bhuri's foot, and at the tyre again.
'Uncle,' she said. 'Why does your wheel sink and Bhuri's foot does not?'
'She is much lighter than the jeep,' said Karim, not looking up.

'She is not,' said Gauri. 'Dadaji weighed her at the fair. She is six hundred kilos.' She crouched and put her hand flat on Bhuri's foot. 'Look at it. It is wide, and it is soft. When she steps, it spreads out like a roti on a tava.'
Revathi bent down. The pad of the camel's foot was as wide as a dinner plate, and when Bhuri lifted it, it was a round shape. When she put it down, it flattened and widened.

'Now look at your tyre,' said Gauri. 'It is hard, and round, and only this wide.' She showed a hand's width. 'All of the jeep sits on four small patches. Bhuri's weight is shared over four big patches. So her patches are pushed less.'
Karim stopped digging. 'You think I should have a bigger tyre?'

'You do not need a bigger one,' said Gauri slowly. 'You need to make this one wider. When the tractor comes for the wheat, my uncle lets the air out of the tyres on sand. He says they get fat and sit on top.'
Revathi laughed in surprise. 'She is right. I read this once. A softer tyre flattens where it touches the ground. The patch gets bigger, so the same weight is pushed over more sand.'

Karim looked at the girl, and at the camel's calm foot, and he knelt at the back wheel. With a small stick, he pressed the valve. The air hissed out for a long time. The tyre sagged and bulged out at the bottom, as if it were sitting down. He did the same at all four wheels.

Then he started the engine and pressed the pedal very gently. The jeep rocked once, twice, and then rolled out of its pits as if the sand had changed its mind. It climbed the slope and stopped at the top, where the ground was hard again. Gauri whooped. Bhuri, who had watched everything with her long eyelashes, calmly chewed.

At the dhani, Revathi gave the calf her injection, and by evening the little one was drinking. Karim pumped his tyres up again with the hand pump, and said he would never drive onto sand with tyres full of air again.

A week later, it rained. The Thar does not rain often, and the sand turned to a wet, shining clay. Gauri was leading Bhuri to the well when the camel's feet began to slide. Her legs slipped outwards, and she stood trembling with her feet far apart, her wide pads skating on the mud. Gauri held her rope and spoke to her softly, until she found her footing, one slow step at a time.
'She is clever on sand,' said Dadaji, who had come out to help. 'But on wet clay, she is like a child in new slippers.'
Gauri stroked Bhuri's neck. 'The same foot,' she said. 'It is good for sand and no good for mud.'
'That is how it is with feet,' said Dadaji, 'and with most things.'
story.epiphany: The camel's wide foot and the softer tyre do the same job: they spread a weight over more ground. The same foot that floats on sand slides on clay, so a body part is good for one kind of place.
ask: Why did the jeep sink when Karim pressed the pedal harder?
What did Gauri notice about Bhuri's foot, and how did the tyre change?
Why was Bhuri good on the sand, and not on the wet clay?
What is a place where a wide foot would be a problem?

how_we_found_out.story: For centuries, travellers said that a camel's hump was a tank of water, and some said that a camel kept water in her stomach too. In 1956, a Norwegian-American scientist named Knut Schmidt-Nielsen took a team to Beni Abbes in the Algerian Sahara. His wife, Bodil Schmidt-Nielsen, also a scientist, worked with him. They weighed camels every day as they went without water in the summer, took their temperatures, and measured everything that went in and out. The camels lost about a quarter of their weight, and it was water from the whole body. When they were allowed to drink, they took back the lost water in one long drink. The hump was fat. And the camels let their temperature rise by day and fall by night, and so saved the water they would have sweated away.
how_we_found_out.who: Knut Schmidt-Nielsen and Bodil Schmidt-Nielsen, with colleagues, in the Sahara
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People thought that the hump or the stomach was a tank of water. The team showed that the hump is fat, and that the camel's real trick is to lose less water. Her body temperature swings, her nose catches water from her breath, and her blood cells can swell after a big drink.

roots.context: We have looked at three bodies and the problems they solve. Now we ask what these odd bodies tell us about who we are, what life is and what the world is.

deep_truth.truth: No body part is simply good. Each one is a deal between what it gives and what it costs. A camel keeps all her fat in one hump, so the rest of her body can stay cool. An octopus has no bones, so she can squeeze through a crack, but swimming tires her.
deep_truth.habit: We rank animals as simple or advanced, strong or weak, as if one body could be the best at everything. A body is good for one way of life, and it pays for that somewhere else.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Ice Test, the same cloth slowed melting when it was spread all over and hardly at all when it was in one lump. A camel's fat, spread all over, would trap heat. In one lump, it leaves the rest of her free to cool. The camel's wide pad floats on sand and slips on clay.

three.who_am_i: Your feet, your back and your hands are answers to problems too, and they have prices too. You are an animal with a body made of trade-offs, like a camel or an octopus.
three.what_is_life: To stay alive, every animal solves the same few problems each day: food, water, air, movement, warmth and safety. A body is a long, shared answer to them.
three.what_is_this_world: The same Earth sets different problems in different places. Hot sand, hard wood and cold salt water ask for very different bodies.

roots.thread: A foot and the ground it walks on fit each other, like a key and a lock. Sand has shaped the camel's foot, and the camel's foot has shaped how she moves on sand. Wood, water and rock did the same for the woodpecker's beak and the octopus's arms. This is the one world becoming many bodies, each shaped by the place it lives in. Nothing in this is a plan. It is many small differences, slowly kept or lost.

teachings.teaching: The text says that creatures are born from food, live by food and return into food. In this teaching, a body is food made into a living being for a while.
teachings.link: A camel's hump is fat, which is sunlight stored by plants, eaten by a camel and kept for a hard time. Her body is built from food, and her fat is food kept for later.

teachings.teaching: The Chinese teacher Zhuangzi said that every creature and tool has a use and a limit. A battering ram can break a city gate but cannot plug a small hole. A fine racehorse is poor at catching rats, and a cat is good at it. An owl sees a hair at night but not a mountain by day.
teachings.link: A wide pad is good on sand and poor on clay. A soft octopus is good in a crack and poor on a long swim. No body is the best at everything.

teachings.source: Udana 6.4 (the story of the blind men and the elephant, in the Pali scriptures)
teachings.teaching: Blind men each touched a different part of an elephant and each told a different story, so that they quarrelled. Each was right about the part and wrong about the whole. The Jains call this many-sidedness, anekantavada.
teachings.link: An octopus's arm tastes a stone, a woodpecker's tongue finds insects hidden in wood, and a camel's foot feels the sand. Each body meets one world from its own side.

science.text: Fat, the camel's store, is sunlight kept by plants, made into food and then into fat. A gram of fat holds about twice the energy of a gram of sugar.

In 2012, a group of scientists signed the Cambridge Declaration on Consciousness, saying that many animals, including octopuses, have the brain structures that make conscious experience possible. Not every scientist agrees, and what an octopus feels is still an open question.

other_view.view: An octopus's arm tasting a stone, or reaching for food after it is cut off, is a reflex made of nerve signals. It shows a clever body, they say, but not a feeling in the arm. They would say that we need more evidence before saying that an arm, or even a whole octopus, feels anything.

practice.title: Feel your feet
practice.say: Take off your chappals and stand on a firm floor. Spread your toes wide and feel the floor under your whole foot. Now rise slowly onto your toes. Feel the push gather into a small patch. Come back down, and breathe out. Where is the push gentle, and where is it strong? Your foot is an answer to a problem too.
practice.kid: Take off your chappals. Stand on the floor and spread your toes. Feel the floor. Now stand on tiptoe. Where is the push strongest? Come back down and breathe out slowly.

ask: Is a body made to fit a place, or does a place make the body?
If every body is a deal, what is yours giving up?
When an octopus's arm tastes a stone, who is tasting?
Is there a body that is simply better than all the others?

games.title: Part, Problem, Price: a card game
games.context: This is a card game. Each card shows an animal and one of her odd body parts. You say what problem the part solves and what it might cost the animal.

setup.art: Twenty-four cards shuffled into a face-down pile in the middle of a table, with a pencil and a score sheet beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards. Shuffle them into a pile.

setup.art: A child reading the front of a card that says 'Camel: a big hump of fat on her back', with a thought bubble saying 'Problem?' and another saying 'Price?'.
setup.caption: 2. Read the front of the top card. Say the problem and guess the price.

setup.art: The card turned over, showing the problem and the price, with a pencil marking two points on a score sheet.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card over. Score a point for each part you got right.

printables.title: 24 two-sided cards: an animal and a body part on the front, and the problem and the price on the back

items.f: Camel: a big hump of fat on her back.
items.b: Problem: food can be scarce for weeks, and fat all over her body would trap heat. Price: the hump is heavy to carry, and it flops when food is short.

items.f: Camel: wide, soft pads under her feet.
items.b: Problem: sinking into loose sand. The wide pad shares her weight over more sand. Price: the pad slips on wet clay.

items.f: Camel: her body temperature goes up to about 41 degrees by day.
items.b: Problem: sweating wastes scarce water. A hotter body needs less sweating. Price: it works best in dry air with cool nights, where she can cool down again.

items.f: Camel: double eyelashes and nostrils that can close.
items.b: Problem: blowing sand in her eyes and nose. Price: with the nostrils closed she cannot breathe or smell, so she can only close them for a short time.

items.f: Woodpecker: two toes forward, two toes back, and a stiff tail.
items.b: Problem: clinging to a straight trunk without falling backwards. Price: she is clumsy on the ground, and her tail feathers wear against rough bark.

items.f: Woodpecker: a chisel beak and strong neck muscles.
items.b: Problem: opening hard wood to reach food inside. Price: hammering uses a lot of energy, so she must find plenty of insects every day.

items.f: Woodpecker: a long, sticky tongue that curls round her skull.
items.b: Problem: reaching insects deep in narrow tunnels. Price: she depends on insects in wood, and goes hungry if the trees die.

items.f: Woodpecker: a nest hole chiselled into a tree.
items.b: Problem: a dry, safe place for the eggs. Price: she needs big, old or dead trees, so she cannot live where there are none.

items.f: Octopus: a body with no bones.
items.b: Problem: hiding in cracks and gaps. Price: she has no armour and no stiff levers, so she cannot run or swim far.

items.f: Octopus: a jet of water from a funnel.
items.b: Problem: escaping a hunter very fast. Price: jet swimming tires her quickly, because the heart that feeds her body slows down.

items.f: Octopus: three hearts and blue blood.
items.b: Problem: carrying oxygen in cold sea water. Price: blue blood carries less oxygen than red blood in warm water, so she tires easily.

items.f: Octopus: eight arms lined with suckers that taste.
items.b: Problem: finding food in dark cracks by touch. Price: so many arms need a huge number of nerve cells, and nerves cost a lot of food energy.

items.f: Giraffe: a very long neck.
items.b: Problem: reaching leaves high up in trees. Price: she needs a very strong heart to push blood up to her head, and it is hard for her to drink.

items.f: House gecko: tiny hairs on her toes.
items.b: Problem: walking up walls and across the ceiling. Price: dust and water on the hairs make her sticky grip weaker.

items.f: Elephant: big, thin ears.
items.b: Problem: cooling down in the heat, because blood in thin ears loses heat to the air. Price: thin ears tear easily.

items.f: Buffalo: a stomach with four rooms.
items.b: Problem: digesting tough grass, with help from microbes. Price: it is slow, and she must spend hours chewing her cud.

items.f: Snake: no legs and a very bendy backbone.
items.b: Problem: slipping into burrows, cracks and grass. Price: she cannot carry anything, and she must swallow her food whole.

items.f: Bat: wings of skin stretched over long fingers.
items.b: Problem: catching insects in the air at night. Price: she walks very badly on the ground.

items.f: Kingfisher: a long, straight beak and a head-first dive.
items.b: Problem: spearing fish under the water. Price: she needs clear water to see the fish, and goes hungry in muddy water.

items.f: Crow: a strong beak that suits many foods.
items.b: Problem: finding food in a city where it changes every day. Price: she is not the best at any one food. A sunbird sips nectar better, and an eagle tears meat better.

items.f: Sunbird: a thin, curved beak.
items.b: Problem: sipping nectar from deep flowers. Price: she depends on flowers with the right shape, and has trouble when there are none.

items.f: Human: an upright back and two legs.
items.b: Problem: freeing the hands to carry and to make tools. Price: many people get backache and sore hips.

items.f: Human: a big brain.
items.b: Problem: learning, planning and making things. Price: the brain is about 2 parts in 100 of the body's weight, but it uses about 20 parts in 100 of the body's energy.

items.f: Peacock: a long, bright tail.
items.b: Problem: attracting a peahen. Price: the tail is heavy and easy for hunters to see, so it makes flying and hiding harder.

printables.title: A score sheet with a row for each player
items: Player name. Problem points. Price points. Total.
Write one line per round. A card is worth up to 2 points: 1 for the problem, 1 for the price.

rules: Shuffle the cards and put them face down in a pile.
The first player turns over the top card but shows only the front. She reads it aloud.
She says what problem the part solves, and guesses one price it might have.
She turns the card over and reads the back. She scores 1 point if she was close on the problem, and 1 point if she was close on the price.
Any other player may add a better answer. If it is better, that player also scores a point.
Play passes to the left. When the pile is empty, or after 12 cards if time is short, add up the points. The highest score wins.
Playing alone: draw 12 cards and score yourself. Try to beat your own score the next time.

flow.do: Cut out the 24 cards and the score sheet. Shuffle the cards and put them face down. Each player gets a pencil.
flow.say: We have 24 cards. Each one shows an animal and one odd body part. Your job is to say what problem it solves and what it might cost the animal.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Shuffle them. Put them face down. Each card has an animal and a part.
flow.parent: Print the cards on both sides of a page, if you can, with the fronts and backs lined up. If you cannot print, copy each card by hand onto a paper slip, or read the front aloud from the screen and the back afterwards. A grown-up cuts with scissors. One child with a parent: both play. Two to four children: take turns round the table.
flow.context: This is the first step of Part, Problem, Price. You set up the game.

flow.do: Play one practice card together. Turn over the top card and read the front aloud. Say the problem and the price before you look at the back.
flow.say: Practice card. Read the front, but do not look at the back. What problem might this part solve? What might it cost? Say both, and then we will check.
flow.kid: Read the front. Say the problem. Say a price. Then turn the card over.

check.q: Practice card: a camel's wide, soft pads. What is the price?
check.why: The wide pad floats on sand, but on wet clay it has nothing to grip. Picking 'sink in sand' mixes up the problem and the price. The pad solves the sinking. If you picked 'heavy', remember that the pad spreads the weight and does not add much.

flow.parent: A price can be a plain cost, a place where the part is no use, or a thing the animal has to give up. It does not have to be a disaster.
flow.context: This is a practice round. You play one card together and learn what a price is.

flow.do: Take turns. Turn over the top card, say the problem and a price, then read the back. Score points. Keep going until 12 cards are done in all, or until the pile is empty if you have time.
flow.say: Your turn. Read the front. Tell us the problem it solves and one price. Then we read the back. One point for each part you got close.
flow.kid: Take a card. Say the problem and a price. Then read the back. Score your points.

ask.q: Why might this part be a problem in a different place?
good: A camel's wide pad would slip on mud.
A bat's wings are poor for walking.
A big brain needs a lot of food.

flow.parent: Be generous. If the child's answer is close in meaning, give the point. Ask for a reason, not just a word.
flow.context: In this step you play the game. You say a problem and a price for each card.

flow.do: Add up the points. Choose the card you liked best, and tell the others why.
flow.say: Add up the points. Which card surprised you the most? Why?
flow.kid: Add up your points. Which card surprised you most? Why?

check.q: Which sentence best matches what the cards show?
options: Every body part gains something and costs something
Big animals are better than small ones
check.why: Every card had a price. No animal had a part that was good for everything. Picking 'perfect' forgets the prices. Picking 'big is better' is not shown by any card.

flow.context: This is the last step of Part, Problem, Price. You add up the scores and think about what the cards showed.

experiments.title: Ice Test: does it matter where the fat goes?
experiments.question: A camel has fat in one hump. Does the same amount of insulation keep a block of ice cold when it is spread all over, when it is lumped in one place, and when it is missing?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess which block of ice will melt the least and which will melt the most. Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: The three ice blocks come from three identical cups and start at the same size. Blocks B and C get two pieces of cloth of exactly the same size and thickness. All three sit side by side in the same room for the same time. Only one thing differs. Block A has no cloth, block B has the cloth all around, and block C has the cloth lumped on top. Block A is the control.
results_table: Height of meltwater in the glass (cm)

schedule.what: Fill three identical cups with water and freeze them overnight. Make your guess and give a reason.
Do the Ice Test, measure the water and draw your model.

materials.item: 3 identical small plastic cups, each filled with 100 millilitres of water and frozen
3 identical steel katoris, or small bowls, labelled A, B and C
2 pieces of dry old cotton cloth or thin hand towel, each exactly the same size and kind, about 30 centimetres square
a tall, narrow glass, such as a tea glass (or a measuring jug marked in millilitres)
a ruler marked in centimetres and millimetres
a timer or a clock, a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Use plastic cups in the freezer, never glass, which can crack. A grown-up helps to take the ice blocks out of the cups, and never uses a knife on a stuck block. Do not hold an ice block in your bare hands for long, because it can sting your skin. Wipe up any water on the floor.
experiments.record: Write the height of the meltwater for each block, and rank the blocks from least to most melted. Then draw a model: a camel with the fat spread all over, and a camel with the fat in a hump, with arrows showing where the heat escapes.
experiments.context: In this experiment you use three blocks of ice and the same cloth in two different ways. You find out whether insulation works the same when it is spread out and when it is lumped.

setup.art: Three identical plastic cups of water in a freezer, with the labels A, B and C on masking tape.
setup.caption: 1. The day before, freeze three identical cups of water.

setup.art: Three ice blocks in three steel katoris in a row, labelled A, B and C.
setup.caption: 2. Tip one ice block into each katori.

setup.art: Block A bare, block B wrapped all around in cloth, and block C with the same cloth lumped in a pad on top only.
setup.caption: 3. A stays bare. Wrap B all over. Put the same cloth in a pad on top of C.

setup.art: A clock set for 25 minutes next to the three katoris on a table away from the Sun and the fan.
setup.caption: 4. Set a timer for 25 minutes and leave them side by side.

setup.art: A child squeezing the cloth over a katori and pouring the water into a tall narrow glass with a ruler beside it.
setup.caption: 5. Pour each block's water into the glass. Measure the height.

flow.do: Fill three identical cups with 100 millilitres of water each. Label them A, B and C. Put them in the freezer overnight. Ask for a guess and a reason before the cups go in.
flow.say: Tomorrow we will melt three ice blocks. One stays bare. One is wrapped all around in cloth. One gets the same cloth lumped on top. Which melts the least? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Tomorrow we melt three ice blocks. Which melts the least? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Which block will melt the least, and why?
good: The wrapped one, because the cloth keeps the warm air away.
The one with the cloth on top, because the cloth is thick.
They will all melt the same, because the cloth is the same.

flow.parent: Do not correct any guess. Write it down with the reason. Check that all three cups are the same size and have the same amount of water. Use plastic cups that can go in a freezer. One child with a parent: the child guesses and wraps, the parent pours and keeps time. Two to four children: share one set of three blocks and split the jobs (one wraps B, one wraps C, one keeps time, one measures), then swap jobs for a second round. With four children, two pairs can run two sets and compare answers. Stand the cups upright on a flat shelf. If the power goes off overnight, freeze them again.
flow.wait: Leave the cups in the freezer overnight.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Ice Test. You freeze the blocks and guess what will happen.

flow.do: Hold each cup under the tap for 5 seconds. Tip the ice block into the katori with the same letter. Check that the blocks look the same size.
flow.say: Run the tap on the outside of each cup for 5 seconds. Then tip the block out into its katori. Do the blocks look the same?
flow.kid: Run the tap on the outside of a cup. Tip the ice into its katori. Do this three times.
flow.parent: A grown-up helps if a block sticks. If one block is clearly smaller, swap it for a spare, or the test is not fair. Freeze one spare cup. If a block will not come out, run the tap a little longer.

check.q: Why must the three ice blocks be the same size?
options: So that any difference in melting comes from the cloth
check.why: If one block were bigger, it would melt less, whatever was on it. We could not tell if the cloth or the size made the difference. A fair test changes only one thing.

flow.context: In this step you take the ice out of the cups and check that the blocks are alike.

flow.do: Leave block A bare. Wrap block B in one cloth, all around its sides, top and bottom. Fold the other cloth into a thick pad and lay it on top of block C only.
flow.say: Block A stays bare. Block B is wrapped in one cloth, all around. Block C gets the other cloth, folded into a pad on top. The sides of C stay bare.
flow.kid: A stays bare. Wrap B all over in one cloth. Fold the other cloth. Put it on top of C.
flow.parent: Both cloths must be the same size and the same kind. Wrap B loosely, as a blanket. Do not press the cloth hard against the ice. C's cloth sits on the top, and the sides are open. Use dry cloth. If the cloth is thin, fold both cloths in two the same way.

check.q: Why do B and C get cloths of exactly the same size?
options: So the only difference is where the cloth is, all around or on top
check.why: B and C have the same amount of cloth. If they melt differently, the reason must be where the cloth sits. If C had a thicker cloth, we would not know whether the place or the amount made the difference.

flow.context: In this step you dress the three blocks. The amount of cloth is the same for B and C, and only its place changes.

flow.do: Put the three katoris side by side on a table, away from the fan and from sunlight. Set a timer for 25 minutes. Write down the time.
flow.say: Put all three side by side, out of the Sun and the fan. Set the timer for 25 minutes. Now we wait.
flow.kid: Put the katoris side by side. Not in the Sun. Set a timer for 25 minutes.
flow.parent: If your room is very hot, melting is fast. If a block has melted completely before the time is up, use 15 minutes next time. If it is cold, melting is slow, so use 40 minutes.
flow.context: In this step you start the clock. All three blocks sit in the same place for the same time.

flow.do: While you wait, draw two camels. Draw one with fat spread all over her body, and one with fat in a hump. Draw arrows for the heat leaving each camel. Do not touch the blocks.
flow.say: While we wait, draw two camels. One has fat spread all over her body. One has fat in a hump. Draw arrows where you think her body heat can leave.
flow.kid: Draw two camels. One has fat all over. One has a hump. Draw arrows for heat leaving.

ask.q: On which camel can the heat leave more easily, and why?
good: The one with the hump, because the rest of her skin is thin.
The one with fat all over has a thick blanket that holds the heat in.

flow.parent: This is the child's own model. Any drawing with a reason is good. Do not explain the answer yet. Let the ice give the evidence.
flow.context: This is a drawing step. You draw your own model of a camel while the ice melts.

flow.do: When the timer rings, lift block A out. Pour the water from katori A into the tall glass. Measure its height with the ruler. Do the same for B and C. Squeeze each cloth over its katori first.
flow.say: Time is up. Lift out each block. For B and C, squeeze the cloth over the katori. Then pour all the water into the tall glass and measure how high it goes.
flow.kid: Lift out the block. Squeeze the cloth. Pour the water into the glass. Measure the height. Do A, B and C.
flow.parent: Empty and wipe the glass before each block. Measure to the nearest millimetre. Do not worry if your numbers are small. The pattern is what matters. With a measuring jug, read millilitres instead, and change the table heading.
flow.context: In this step you measure how much each block melted. More water means more melting.

flow.do: Fill in the table. Rank the blocks. Then ask for the three parts: what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: Which block melted the least? Which melted the most? Which two were closest? Now tell me three things. What did you think? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Fill in the table. Which block melted the least? Which melted the most? Why?

ask.q: What do you notice about A and C?
good: They melted almost the same.
The cloth on top did not help much.
C melted a little less than A.

ask.q: Which block is like a camel with fat all over, and which is like a camel with a hump?
good: B is fat all over. C is the hump.
The hump leaves the sides bare, so heat gets in or out there.

flow.parent: In most homes block B melts the least. Blocks A and C come out close, and C melts a little less than A. As a rough guide only, in a warm room a bare block gives about 20 to 40 millilitres of meltwater in 25 minutes, and a wrapped one about half of that. Your numbers will differ. If all three are within 2 millimetres of each other, the test showed no difference: say so honestly, then repeat with 40 minutes or thicker cloth. Let the child say what the test shows before you explain. The model is honest only in part: the ice is colder than the room, and a camel is hotter than the night air. But a layer slows heat in both directions.

check.q: Which result best matches this idea? The same cloth works as a good coat only when it is spread all over.
check.why: Block B has the cloth all around, and it melted the least. Block C has the same cloth, but heat reached it from the open sides. A and C usually melt almost the same, because heat reaches C through its open sides.

flow.context: In this step you read your results and say what they show, with a claim, evidence and reasoning.

experiments.title: Foot Test: why does a camel not sink in the sand?
experiments.question: If the same weight stands on a small foot, a medium foot and a wide foot, how deep does each sink into soft ground?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess which foot will sink the deepest and which will hardly sink at all. Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: The weight is the same every time, a steel tumbler with 300 millilitres of water. The soft ground is the same slab of dough, smoothed flat before each try. Each foot stays down for 30 seconds. Only the width of the foot changes. We try each foot twice, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: about 1 kilogram of atta, mixed with water into a soft dough like the dough for chapati (or loose dry atta in a deep tray, smoothed flat, if the dough is too firm)
a rolling pin and a baking tray or large thali, at least 25 centimetres wide
1 steel tumbler with 300 millilitres of water in it, as the weight
a bottle cap or jar lid about 3 centimetres wide, for the small foot (open side down, so its ring presses the dough)
a flat plate, thali or plastic lid about 18 centimetres wide, for the wide foot (the lighter the better)
a spoon, a ruler, a toothpick, a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: The dough is made of wheat. Do not eat it raw, and wash hands afterwards. If anyone is allergic to wheat, use clay or play-dough instead. Wipe up any spilt water.
experiments.record: Write the width of each foot and the depth of each dent in millimetres. Work out the average for each foot. Then draw the three dents side by side, to scale.
experiments.context: In this experiment the same weight stands on three feet of different widths. You find out how the width of a foot changes how deep it sinks.

setup.art: A baking tray with a slab of soft dough about 2 centimetres thick, rolled smooth, and a rolling pin beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Roll the dough into a smooth, flat slab in the tray.

setup.art: Three feet in a row: a bottle cap, a steel tumbler base and a wide steel plate, with their widths written beside them.
setup.caption: 2. Meet the three feet: small, medium and wide.

setup.art: A steel tumbler of water balanced on a bottle cap on the dough, with one fingertip steadying it at the side.
setup.caption: 3. Stand the tumbler on the small foot for 30 seconds.

setup.art: The steel plate lying flat on the dough with the tumbler of water standing in the middle of it.
setup.caption: 4. Try the same tumbler on the wide plate.

setup.art: A toothpick standing in a dent in the dough, with a pencil laid across the top and a finger pinching the toothpick.
setup.caption: 5. Measure the depth of each dent with a toothpick and a pencil.

flow.do: Show your child the three feet: the bottle cap, the tumbler base and the plate. Measure the width of each with the ruler. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: The same tumbler of water will stand on three feet. A small cap, its own base and a wide plate. Which foot will sink deepest into the dough? Which will sink the least? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Meet the three feet. Which one sinks the deepest? Which hardly sinks? Why?

ask.q: Which foot do you think will sink the deepest, and why?
good: The small cap, because all the weight is on a tiny patch.
The wide plate, because it is heavy.
They will all sink the same, because the weight is the same.

flow.parent: Write the widths in the table. Do not correct any guess. Many children think that the plate is heavier so it sinks more. Let the dough show them. One child with a parent: the child places the weight and counts the seconds, the parent measures. Two to four children: split the jobs (place the weight, count 30 seconds, measure the dent, write the table) and swap jobs for the second try, so every child measures at least once.

check.q: The tumbler has the same weight on all three feet. Which foot will push on the dough with the greatest pressure?
options: The small cap, because the weight is shared over the smallest patch
The wide plate, because it is the biggest
All three, because the weight is equal
check.why: Pressure is the weight divided by the area. The same weight on a small area gives a big pressure. Picking the plate usually means thinking that bigger means heavier. Picking all three means forgetting that the patch is different.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Foot Test. You look at the three feet and guess.

flow.do: Roll the dough into a slab about 2 centimetres thick in the tray. Smooth the top with the back of a spoon. Fill the tumbler with 300 millilitres of water.
flow.say: Roll the dough flat, about two fingers thick. Smooth it with the back of a spoon. This is our soft ground, like loose sand. Now fill the tumbler to 300 millilitres. This is our weight.
flow.kid: Roll the dough flat. Smooth it. Fill the tumbler with 300 millilitres of water.
flow.parent: The dough should be soft enough to take a dent from a gentle press, but not sticky. If it is too hard, add a little water. If you cannot see a dent from the cap, add more water to the tumbler, and use the same amount every time. If the dough sticks to the plate, dust the plate with a little dry atta. Measure the dent as soon as you lift the weight off, because dough springs back a little.
flow.context: In this step you make the soft ground and the weight. They stay the same through the whole test.

flow.do: Put the bottle cap flat on the dough, open side down. Balance the tumbler on it, steadying it with one fingertip at the side. Wait 30 seconds. Lift off both. Measure the dent with the toothpick and pencil. Smooth the dough and try again.
flow.say: Cap first. Put the tumbler on top and steady it with one finger, without pressing down. Count to thirty. Lift off. Slide the toothpick into the dent, and pinch it where it meets the pencil. Measure it on the ruler.
flow.kid: Put the cap on the dough. Stand the tumbler on it. Wait 30 seconds. Measure the dent.
flow.parent: To measure: lay a pencil across the dent. Slide the toothpick straight down to the bottom. Pinch the toothpick where it meets the pencil and lay it along the ruler. Smooth the dough with the spoon between tries. Do two tries.
flow.context: In this step you test the small foot twice and measure how deep it sinks.

flow.do: Smooth the dough. Stand the tumbler on its own base on a fresh patch for 30 seconds. Lift it off. Measure the dent. Do it twice.
flow.say: Now the tumbler on its own base, the medium foot. Wait thirty seconds. Lift off and measure the dent. Then smooth the dough and do it again.
flow.kid: Stand the tumbler on its own base. Wait 30 seconds. Measure the dent. Do it twice.
flow.parent: Remember to measure the width of the tumbler base and write it in the table. If a dent is too faint to measure, write 0 and the word 'faint'.
flow.context: In this step you test the medium foot twice, with the tumbler standing on its own base.

flow.do: Smooth the dough. Lay the plate flat on it. Stand the tumbler in the middle of the plate for 30 seconds. Lift both off. Look for a dent and measure it. Do it twice.
flow.say: Last, the wide foot. Lay the plate on the dough and stand the tumbler in the middle. Wait thirty seconds. Lift off. Is there a dent? If there is, measure it.
flow.kid: Lay the plate on the dough. Stand the tumbler on it. Wait 30 seconds. Is there a dent?
flow.parent: A dent from the plate may be very faint or none at all. Write 0 if you can see none. That is a true result and not a failure. The plate weighs a little more than the cap, but that is small next to how much wider it is. As a rough guide only, the cap often leaves a dent of a few millimetres, the tumbler base 1 or 2 millimetres, and the plate none.
flow.context: In this step you test the wide foot twice. The plate may leave hardly any dent at all.

flow.do: Work out the average dent for each foot. Rank the feet from deepest to shallowest. Ask for three things: what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: Add the two tries for each foot and halve. Which foot sank the deepest? Which the least? Now tell me three things. What did you think? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Find the average dent for each foot. Which sank deepest? Which sank least? Why?

ask.q: The weight was the same each time. Why did the dents differ?
good: The same weight was shared over a bigger patch on the plate.
A small foot pushes harder on each bit of dough.

ask.q: How is this like a camel in the sand?
good: Her wide pad shares her weight over more sand, so she sinks less.
A thin hoof would sink like the cap.

flow.parent: In most homes the dents get shallower as the foot gets wider, and the plate leaves almost none. Your numbers will differ. The pattern is what matters. Let the child give the reasoning before you add the word pressure.

check.q: Why does a camel's wide foot sink less than a narrow hoof of the same animal weight?
options: The weight is shared over a bigger patch of sand, so each bit is pushed less
check.why: The weight of the camel is the same. A wider pad spreads it over a bigger area, so the push on each small patch of sand is smaller. A wide foot is not lighter. If you picked 'harder', remember that the soft pad squashes and spreads.

flow.context: In this step you read your results and explain them, with a claim, evidence and reasoning.

activities.title: Squeeze Test: how small a hole can a soft body pass?

materials.item: a piece of stiff cardboard from a carton, about 30 by 30 centimetres
a ruler, a pencil and a pair of strong scissors (a grown-up pokes a starter hole with the scissor tip, then cuts)
a ball of soft atta dough about 4 centimetres wide
a marble (kanche) or a hard bead about 1.5 centimetres wide
a small hard ball about 4 centimetres wide, such as a rubber or plastic toy ball, or a smooth stone

activities.safety: A grown-up cuts the holes with strong scissors, and the point is sharp. Keep the scissors away from small children. Keep the marble away from children under 4. Dough is made of wheat. Do not eat it raw, and wash hands afterwards. If anyone is allergic to wheat, use clay or play-dough instead.
activities.record: Write which holes each body passed, and which it did not. Draw the three bodies and the smallest hole each passed.
activities.context: In this activity you push three bodies through holes of different sizes. You find out what sets the smallest hole that a soft body can pass, as an octopus does.

setup.art: A cardboard sheet with five squares drawn in a row, with sides 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 centimetres, each labelled.
setup.caption: 1. Draw five squares on the cardboard. A grown-up cuts them out.

setup.art: Three bodies in a row: a hard ball, a plain dough ball and a dough ball with a marble inside.
setup.caption: 2. Make three bodies: a hard ball, a dough ball, and a dough ball with a marble inside.

setup.art: A child pushing the dough ball through a small square hole in the cardboard, the dough coming out in a worm on the other side.
setup.caption: 3. Try to push each body through each hole. Start with the biggest hole.

flow.do: Draw five squares in a row on the cardboard, with sides 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 centimetres. A grown-up cuts them out. Press the marble into the middle of the dough ball and close the dough around it.
flow.say: We will test three bodies. A hard ball, a plain dough ball, and a dough ball with a marble inside. Which is the smallest hole each one can pass? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Draw five squares. A grown-up cuts them out. Hide a marble inside a dough ball.

ask.q: Which body will fit through the smallest hole, and why?
good: The dough, because it is soft and can squash.
The dough with the marble, but not through a hole smaller than the marble.
The hard ball can only fit the big holes.

flow.parent: Make the plain dough ball the same size as the dough ball with the marble inside. Write the guesses down before the test. Do not correct them. One child with a parent: the child pushes and the parent writes. Two to four children: share the cardboard, and let each child make and push their own dough ball, with a marble inside or not. Take turns, and one child records.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Squeeze Test. You make the holes and the bodies, and guess.

flow.do: For each body, start with the biggest hole. Try to push it through. If it goes, try the next smaller hole. Write the smallest hole it passed. Use the same push each time, with your fingers.
flow.say: Start with the biggest hole. Push the body through, using your fingers. If it goes, try the next hole. Write down the smallest hole it passes.
flow.kid: Push each body through a hole. Start with the biggest. Go smaller. Write the smallest hole.
flow.parent: The dough ball may come out the other side as a long worm. That counts as passing. The hard ball passes only the biggest hole. The marble in the dough should stop it at the 1 centimetre hole, and may also stick at 2 centimetres, because the thin dough round the marble is hard to squeeze. The plain dough may need a firm push at the 1 centimetre hole. Hold the cardboard flat against a table edge. If even the plain dough will not go through, write that down as the result, or add a few drops of water to the dough and try again. Redo any try where the cardboard tears.

check.q: What sets the smallest hole that the dough ball with the marble can pass?
check.why: The soft dough squashes through, but the hard marble does not squash. The marble sets the limit. An octopus's beak does the same job for her: she can pass any gap as wide as her beak.

flow.context: In this step you test each body on the holes and write down what passes.

flow.do: Compare your results with your guesses. Say what the hard part of an octopus is, and what that tells you about the cracks she can enter.
flow.say: Which body went through the smallest hole? What set the limit for the dough with the marble? An octopus has only one big hard part, her beak. What does that tell us about the holes she can use?
flow.kid: Which body passed the smallest hole? What stopped the marble ball? What is hard on an octopus?

ask.q: What is the price of having no bones?
good: No armour to protect her.
Nothing stiff to push or swim far with.
She is easy to bite.

flow.parent: Many octopuses are caught in jars and pots in the sea because they will go into any space that is wider than their beak. Let the child say what the test shows before you add this.
flow.context: In this step you think about what the test shows about the octopus.

activities.title: Tongue Tools: reach the raisin in the crack

materials.item: a tube of stiff paper about 15 centimetres long and 1.2 centimetres wide (roll a sheet round a thick marker pen and tape it), taped shut at one end
5 raisins or small pieces of jaggery
a fork, a thin pencil, a spoon and a straightened paper clip with a tiny hook bent at the end
a thin stick or ice-cream stick with fresh clear tape wrapped round the end, sticky side out
a timer and a pencil

activities.safety: A grown-up checks that the paper clip hook and the stick have blunt ends. Do not put tools near the eyes. Do not use honey for a child under 1 year.
activities.record: Write how many raisins each tool took out in one minute. Draw the best tool and say what is like a woodpecker's tongue.
activities.context: In this activity you try five tools to pull raisins out of a narrow tube. You find out which tool works best, as a woodpecker's tongue does in a crack.

setup.art: A paper tube taped to a board, with five raisins pressed deep inside it and the open end facing the child.
setup.caption: 1. Press five raisins deep into the tube. Tape the tube to a board.

setup.art: Five tools in a row: a fork, a pencil, a spoon, a bent paper clip and a stick with sticky tape on the end.
setup.caption: 2. Lay out the five tools.

setup.art: A child pushing the sticky stick into the tube and pulling out a raisin stuck to it.
setup.caption: 3. Try each tool for one minute. Count the raisins.

flow.do: Press the five raisins to the deep end of the tube. Lay out the five tools. Ask your child which tool will get the most raisins in one minute, and why.
flow.say: A woodpecker has to get insects out of a narrow tunnel in the wood. Here are five tools. Which will get the most raisins out in one minute? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Raisins are deep in a tube. Which of five tools gets the most? Why?

ask.q: Which tool will get the most raisins, and why?
good: The sticky one, because the raisin will stick to it.
The bent paper clip, because the hook can catch a raisin.
The pencil, because it is long.

flow.parent: Do not correct any guess. The fork and spoon may not fit in the tube at all. That is a result. One child with a parent: the parent also tries each tool, so there are two scores to compare. Two to four children: each child tries a tool for one minute while another counts, then swap tools. Make a second tube if you have paper, so two children can work at once.
flow.context: This is the first step of Tongue Tools. You set up the tube and guess.

flow.do: Try each tool for one minute. Count the raisins you pull out. Push the raisins back in before the next tool. Write the number for each tool.
flow.say: One minute for each tool. Count the raisins that come out. Then push them back in for the next tool.
flow.kid: Try each tool for one minute. Count the raisins. Put them back.
flow.parent: The sticky stick or the hook usually wins, depending on your tape and raisins. If the tape will not hold a raisin, use fresh tape, or dab a little honey or sugar syrup on the tip. The pencil may push the raisins further in. Write down exactly what happens. A tool that fails is a result.

check.q: Which tool is most like a woodpecker's tongue?
check.why: A woodpecker's tongue is long, thin and sticky, with a barbed tip, so insects stick to it. The fork and the spoon are too wide for a narrow tunnel.

flow.context: In this step you test the five tools and count how many raisins each one takes out.

flow.do: Look at your numbers. Say which tool was best and why. Ask your child what the tongue of a woodpecker needs to be like.
flow.say: Which tool was best? Which did not work at all? What must a woodpecker's tongue be like to reach an insect deep in a tunnel?
flow.kid: Which tool won? What must a woodpecker's tongue be like?

ask.q: What must a woodpecker's tongue be like?
good: Long and thin.
Sticky.
Able to go far out of her beak.

flow.parent: Tell your child that a woodpecker's tongue can be as long as the beak plus about 10 centimetres in some woodpeckers, and curls round the skull when it is drawn in.
flow.context: In this step you look at the results and think about the tongue of a woodpecker.

activities.title: Window Watch: move, eat and breathe

materials.item: a window, a balcony or a terrace where you can see crows, pigeons, sparrows or squirrels
paper, a pencil and a clipboard or a book to write on
a few grains of rice or a bowl of water to put out for birds, if you like

activities.safety: Do not lean out of a window or climb on a railing to see better. Keep a grown-up with you on a terrace.
activities.record: Draw a table with three columns: How she moves, how she eats, how she breathes or rests. Fill it in for one animal, with a sentence about the odd part you noticed.
activities.context: In this activity you watch one animal from a window for 12 minutes. You note how she moves and eats, and match each part to a problem.

setup.art: A child sitting at a window with a notebook, looking at a crow on the railing.
setup.caption: 1. Find a quiet spot where you can see an animal.

setup.art: An open notebook with a table of three columns: moves, eats, breathes or rests.
setup.caption: 2. Draw a table with three columns.

setup.art: A close-up drawing of a crow's foot gripping a railing and her beak holding a piece of bread.
setup.caption: 3. Draw the part that you think does the job.

flow.do: Draw a table with three columns: how she moves, how she eats, how she breathes or rests. Pick a window or a balcony spot. Ask your child what problems a crow must solve every day.
flow.say: We will watch one animal for twelve minutes. A crow, a pigeon or a squirrel will do. What problems does she have to solve every day? Which body parts do you expect to see at work?
flow.kid: Pick an animal outside. Draw three columns: moves, eats, breathes or rests. What do you expect?
