ask.q: What problems does a crow or pigeon have to solve each day?
good: Finding food.
Staying safe.
Getting from one place to another.
Keeping cool or warm.

flow.parent: A crow is nearly always there in an Indian city, as are pigeons and house sparrows. If none comes, watch an ant or a lizard. Watch from inside if your balcony has no safe railing.
flow.context: This is the first step of Window Watch. You pick an animal and set up your table.

flow.do: Watch for 12 minutes without talking. Write what the animal does. Note how she moves, how she eats and what she does when she rests. Draw her feet and her beak. Count her steps, hops or pecks in one minute, and count again.
flow.say: Watch quietly for twelve minutes. Write what you see. How does she walk or hop? How does she eat? What do her feet and beak look like?
flow.kid: Watch quietly. Write how she moves and eats. Draw her feet and beak.
flow.parent: If you can see her chest rise and fall while she rests, count the rises in 15 seconds. A crow often breathes faster than you. Do not worry if you cannot see it. One child with a parent: the parent writes what the child calls out. Two to four children: each takes one column (moves, eats, rests) and counts, then you put the notes together. If no animal comes, put out a few grains of rice or a bowl of water and wait quietly.
flow.context: In this step you watch the animal and write what you see.

flow.do: For one body part, write the problem it solves and a price. Tell somebody what you found.
flow.say: Pick one part, such as a beak, a foot or a wing. What problem does it solve? What might it cost her? Tell me what you found.
flow.kid: Pick one part. What problem does it solve? What might it cost her?

check.q: A crow has a strong, all-purpose beak. What is a likely price?
options: She is not the best at any one food
check.why: A beak that suits many foods works for all of them, but not as well as a special beak for one food. Picking 'cannot eat at all' or 'cannot fly' does not match what you watched.

flow.context: In this step you match one part of the animal to a problem and a price.

activities.title: Two Hands, Two Jobs: why eight arms are hard

materials.item: 2 pencils and a sheet of paper
a timer

activities.record: Write how long each task took, and which was harder. Draw an octopus with eight arms, and write what each arm is doing.
activities.context: In this activity you try to do two jobs with two hands at once. You find out why an animal with eight arms needs special nerve cells.

setup.art: A child holding a pencil in each hand over a sheet of paper, drawing a circle with one hand and a triangle with the other.
setup.caption: 1. Hold a pencil in each hand.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a circle and a triangle that wobble.
setup.caption: 2. Draw a circle and a triangle at the same time.

setup.art: An octopus drawn with eight arms each doing a different job: one tasting, one holding, one reaching.
setup.caption: 3. Draw an octopus with eight arms doing eight jobs.

flow.do: Draw a circle with your right hand, then a triangle with your left. Time each one. Ask your child to guess how it will look if both hands draw at the same time.
flow.say: First draw a circle with one hand, and a triangle with the other, one after the other. How long does each take? Now, what will happen if you do both at the same time?
flow.kid: Draw a circle. Draw a triangle. Time each one. Now guess: both at once?

ask.q: What will happen if you draw both at the same time, and why?
good: It will be harder, because my brain has to do two things.
It will be messy.
The shapes will get mixed up.

flow.parent: Do not rush. Let the child guess and give a reason before trying. One child with a parent: the parent times and tries too. Two to four children: take turns to draw while another times and scores, then compare scores for one hand at a time against both hands together.
flow.context: This is the first step of Two Hands, Two Jobs. You time two easy drawings, one at a time.

flow.do: Draw the circle and the triangle at the same time, one in each hand. Time it, and score it: 1 point for a round circle and 1 for a triangle with three clear corners. Try once more. Then try patting your head with one hand and rubbing your tummy with the other.
flow.say: Now both at once. A circle in one hand and a triangle in the other. Start together. How does it look? Then try patting your head and rubbing your tummy.
flow.kid: Draw both at once. How do they look? Pat your head and rub your tummy.
flow.parent: Most people find this hard at first. The circle may turn into a triangle, or the other way round. This is normal.

check.q: Why is drawing two shapes at once harder than one at a time?
options: One brain has to guide two different movements together
check.why: In humans, one central brain steers both hands, and the two jobs get mixed up. An octopus has most of her nerve cells in her arms, so each arm has some control of its own.

flow.context: In this step you do both drawings at the same time and notice what goes wrong.

flow.do: Draw an octopus with eight arms, each doing a different job. Say how she could do eight jobs at once if one brain had to steer all eight.
flow.say: An octopus has eight arms. Each one has a lot of its own nerve cells. Draw her doing eight jobs at once. How might she manage it?
flow.kid: Draw an octopus with eight arms. Each arm does a different job.

ask.q: How might an octopus do eight jobs at once?
good: Each arm has some of its own control.
The arms do not wait for the central brain.

flow.parent: About two thirds of an octopus's nerve cells are in her arms. How much each arm decides for herself is still being studied. Do not tell the child the answer is settled.
flow.context: In this step you draw an octopus and think about how she might manage eight arms.

projects.title: My Body Book: three animals, three problems

materials.item: 4 sheets of paper folded into a small book, stapled or tied with thread
pencils and colours
a window or terrace with a view of birds, lizards or ants

projects.safety: Do not touch wild animals, and keep hands away from ants, which can bite. Watch lizards and ants from a distance. Do not lean out of a window, and keep a grown-up with you on a terrace. A grown-up does the stapling.

schedule.what: Make the book. Watch a crow or a pigeon. Fill a page: problem, part, price.
Watch an ant or a house lizard. Fill a page: problem, part, price.
Fill a page about yourself, and a page about the camel, the woodpecker or the octopus. Share your book.

projects.record: A small book with four pages: the bird, the ant or lizard, yourself, and the camel, woodpecker or octopus. Each page has a drawing, a problem, a part and a price.
projects.context: In this project you make a small book of three animals, including you. For each, you write a problem, the part that solves it, and its price.

setup.art: Four sheets of paper folded in half and tied with a thread to make a small book, with 'My Body Book' on the cover.
setup.caption: 1. Fold four sheets into a book. Write a title on the cover.

setup.art: A page of the book showing a crow with arrows to her beak and feet, and three labelled boxes: Problem, Part, Price.
setup.caption: 2. On each page, draw an animal. Label a problem, a part and a price.

setup.art: A child showing the open book to a parent at a table.
setup.caption: 3. On day 3, share your book with someone.

flow.do: Fold the paper into a book. Write the title on the cover. Watch a crow or a pigeon for ten minutes. On the first page draw her and fill in the problem, the part and the price.
flow.say: Let us make a body book. On the first page, draw the animal you watch. Then write three things. A problem she has to solve, the body part that helps, and its price.
flow.kid: Make a small book. Watch a bird. Draw her. Write a problem, a part and a price.

ask.q: What problem does the part you chose solve?
good: Her foot grips the railing so that she does not fall.
Her beak lets her eat many foods.

flow.parent: Help with the words, but let the child choose the part. Any honest guess about the price is fine. Two to four children: each makes their own book, may watch the same bird side by side, and compares what each wrote. If no bird comes, watch a squirrel, a dog or a cow.
flow.context: This is day 1 of the body book. You make the book and fill the first page.

flow.do: Watch an ant or a house lizard for ten minutes. Fill the second page: draw her, and write a problem, a part and a price.
flow.say: Today, watch an ant or a lizard. What does she do? What body part helps her do it? What might it cost her?
flow.kid: Watch an ant or a lizard. Draw her. Write a problem, a part and a price.
flow.parent: Ants and house geckos are common in most Indian homes. Do not touch them. A gecko's toes with tiny hairs are the part to look for.
flow.context: This is day 2 of the body book. You fill the second page with a new animal.

flow.do: Fill a page about your own body. Pick one part, such as a foot or a hand. Write a problem, the part and a price. Fill a last page about the camel, the woodpecker or the octopus. Then share your book.
flow.say: Last day. Pick a part of your own body, and write its problem and its price. Then do the same for the camel, the woodpecker or the octopus. Then show your book to someone.
flow.kid: Do a page for your own body. Do a page for a camel, woodpecker or octopus. Share your book.

check.q: In your book, what do the pages for the crow, the lizard and you have in common?
options: Each part solves a problem and has a price
All the parts are the same
None of the parts has a price
check.why: Every body part you wrote about solves a problem for that animal, and every one costs something. Humans are animals too, and our parts also have prices.

flow.context: This is day 3 of the body book. You finish the book and share it.

challenges.title: Design an Animal for a Place nobody lives in yet
challenges.problem: Choose a place that an animal has not yet settled in. Design an animal that can live there, using only four body parts. For each part, name the problem it solves and the price it has.
constraints: Choose only four body parts for your animal. Each part must solve a problem in the place you chose.
For each part, write one price: a place where it would not work, or something the animal gives up.
The animal must be able to move, eat and breathe in her place.
No part may be magic. Every part must work by something you have seen in real animals.
materials: a list of places: a high, windy mountain top, a muddy river bank, a salty marsh at low tide, a dark cave, a very tall tree
the Part, Problem, Price cards, if you have played the game
general: For a muddy river bank, wide feet or webbed toes spread the weight on the mud, and a long beak probes for worms.
For a mountain top, thick fur or feathers and a big heart for thin air help.
For a dark cave, large ears for hearing, and whiskers for touching, make up for no eyes.
For a tall tree, gripping toes and a long tail for balance, such as a monkey's, help.
creative: A soft body that can squeeze into rock cracks on the mountain, like an octopus, and so be safe from the wind.
Fat stored in a lump on the back, like a camel's hump, so a marsh animal can last through a month when the tide brings no food.
A sticky tongue like a woodpecker's to pull insects from the cracks in a cave wall.
A body that changes colour with the wall of the cave, so hunters cannot see her.
challenges.your_turn: Choose a place and design your own animal with four body parts. Draw her. For each part, write the problem it solves, how it works and its price. Show your design to someone and ask, 'Where would my animal be in trouble?'
challenges.context: In this challenge you design an animal for a place of your choice. You use the idea that every body part answers a problem and has a price.

setup.art: Five cards laid out on a table, each showing a place: a mountain top, a river bank, a marsh, a cave and a tall tree.
setup.caption: 1. Pick a place.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a drawn animal and four arrows pointing to her parts, each with a Problem and Price note.
setup.caption: 2. Draw your animal with four parts. Label each problem and price.

setup.art: A child showing the drawing to a parent, who points at one part and asks a question.
setup.caption: 3. Show your design. Ask, 'Where would she be in trouble?'

flow.do: Pick a place from the list. Write down the problems an animal would face there. Think of food, water, air, moving around, warmth and safety.
flow.say: Pick a place. What problems would an animal have there? Think about food, water, air, getting around, staying warm or cool, and staying safe.
flow.kid: Pick a place. What problems would an animal have there? Write them down.

ask.q: What is the hardest problem in your place?
good: Finding food on bare rock.
Not sinking in mud.
Seeing in the dark.

flow.parent: Let the child choose. Do not suggest answers. Help with spelling and drawing, not ideas.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Design an Animal challenge. You pick a place and list its problems.

flow.do: Choose four body parts that solve four problems. Draw your animal. Next to each part write the problem, and then its price.
flow.say: Choose four parts. For each one, write the problem it solves and the price it has. Draw your animal with all four.
flow.kid: Pick four parts. Draw your animal. Write a problem and a price for each part.
flow.parent: Every part must have a price. If the child is stuck, ask: where would this part not work? What would she have to give up?

check.q: Which is a good price for a very thick coat on an animal on a mountain?
options: She would overheat in a warm place
The coat would never get wet
check.why: A thick coat is a good answer to cold, but it is a trap for heat. Every good part is good only in one kind of place.

flow.context: In this step you design your animal. You write a problem and a price for each of four parts.

flow.do: Show your design to someone. Ask them to find a place where your animal would be in trouble. Write down what they say.
flow.say: Show your animal to someone. Ask them to find a place where she would be in trouble. What did they say?
flow.kid: Show your animal. Ask: where would she be in trouble?

ask.q: Where would your animal be in trouble, and which part is the cause?
good: On the plain, because her wide feet would be useless.
In the heat, because of her thick coat.

flow.parent: A good design is not a perfect one. It is one where the child can say honestly where it fails. Two to four children: all pick the same place, design alone, then swap drawings and look for each other's trouble spots.
flow.context: In this step you share your design and find its weak points.

worksheets.title: Core worksheet: problem, part and price

items.p: What is the best way to start understanding an odd body part?
opts: Ask what problem it solves and what it costs
Ask what colour it is
Ask whether the animal likes it
items.why: An odd part is usually an answer to a problem in the animal's way of life, and every answer has a price. Colour and liking do not tell you what the part is for.

items.p: What is inside a camel's hump?
opts: Fat
Water
Air
items.why: The hump is a lump of fat, which the camel uses for energy when food is scarce. Many people think it is water, but when camels were studied, the water they lost came from their whole body.

items.p: The same amount of fat keeps heat in better when it is spread all over a body than when it is lumped in one place.
items.why: True. Heat can escape from the bare parts of a body with a lump. In the Ice Test, the cloth all around slowed the melting, and the lump on top did little for the open sides.

items.p: The same weight pushes less on the ground when it is spread over a bigger ____.
items.why: Pressure is weight divided by area. A bigger area shares the same weight over more ground, so each small patch is pushed less. This is why a camel's wide foot sinks less in sand.

items.p: Match each animal part to its job.
pairs: Squirts out a jet of water
The only big hard part she has
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each part answers a problem. The pad spreads the camel's weight. The tail works like a third foot. The funnel gives a jet to push the octopus forward. The beak sets the size of the smallest gap she can pass.

items.p: Sort each body part by the problem it helps to solve.
items: fat kept in one hump, so the rest of the skin is thin
a duck's webbed foot on mud
a camel's temperature rising by day
items.a: as given
items.why: Each part has a main job. Fat in a hump leaves bare skin to lose heat. Wide and webbed feet spread weight. A beak and a tongue work together to get food from wood. Letting the body warm up saves sweating.

items.p: Put these in order to show how wide pads could become common in camels.
a: Some calves are born with slightly wider pads
On soft sand, those calves walk farther and find more food
They live longer and have more calves
Their calves inherit the wide pads
After many generations, wide pads are normal
items.why: The small difference comes first. Survival and having young then make it more common, one generation at a time. No camel grew wider pads because she needed them.

items.p: Which one is not true of an octopus, and why? Three hearts, blue blood, bones, a beak.
items.a: Bones, because an octopus has no bones. The other three are true of an octopus.
items.why: An octopus has no skeleton. Her only big hard part is her beak. She has three hearts and blue blood, which carries oxygen with copper.

items.p: A square foot is 2 centimetres on each side. A bigger square foot is 4 centimetres on each side. How many times as big is the area of the bigger foot?
items.why: The small foot has an area of 2 times 2, which is 4 square centimetres. The big foot has 4 times 4, which is 16 square centimetres. 16 divided by 4 is 4. Doubling the width makes the area 4 times as big.

items.p: A friend says, 'A camel's hump is full of water, because camels live in the desert.' What would you say to your friend? Give a reason.
items.a: The hump is fat, not water. The camel uses the fat for energy when food is short. Her real water-saving tricks are letting her body warm up so she sweats less, and catching water from her breath.
items.why: A strong answer says that the hump is fat, and gives at least one reason or piece of evidence. It may also say how a camel really saves water.

items.p: Draw one camel with fat spread all over her body, and one camel with her fat in a hump. Draw arrows for heat leaving each one.
items.a: Two camels. The first has a thick layer all around with few or no arrows. The second has a hump on her back and arrows leaving her bare sides.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that heat leaves through the thin skin on the sides of the camel with a hump, and is held in by the thick layer on the other camel.

items.p: How does a woodpecker keep from falling backwards while she clings to a trunk?
opts: Her stiff tail props her like a third foot
She glues herself to the bark
She holds her breath
items.why: A woodpecker leans on her stiff tail, and her toes grip with two forward and two back. Together they hold her tight against the trunk.

items.p: An octopus can pass through any gap that is wider than her beak.
items.why: True. The beak is her only big hard part. The rest of her body is soft, so it squeezes through. This is why octopuses escape from jars and tanks.

items.p: Choose any animal, including a human. Name one body part, the problem it solves and one price it has.
items.a: A giraffe's long neck helps her reach high leaves. The price is that she needs a very strong heart to push blood up to her head. Or: a human's upright back frees the hands, and the price is backache.
items.why: A strong answer names a real part, a real problem and a real price. The price may be a cost, or a place where the part does not work.

items.p: A woodpecker's tongue is long and ____, so insects stick to it.
items.why: The tip is also barbed. This lets her pull insects out of narrow tunnels in wood.

items.p: Which of these works for the same reason as a camel's wide foot?
opts: A snowshoe
A sharp nail
A knife blade
items.why: A snowshoe is wide, so it spreads a person's weight over more snow, and the snow holds. A nail and a knife do the opposite. They put all the push on a tiny patch.

worksheets.title: Stretch worksheet: gains, costs and different answers

items.p: In an ice test, a block with cloth all around melts least. A block with the same cloth lumped on top melts almost as much as a bare block. What does this show?
opts: Insulation helps only where it covers
Cloth makes ice melt faster
Cloth on top works better than cloth all around
items.why: Heat reaches the block through the parts that stay bare. A lump on the top does little for the sides. This is why a camel's fat in a hump does not trap the heat of her whole body.

items.p: Why does a camel's temperature rising by day save her water?
opts: A body allowed to warm up does not need to sweat as much
A hot body drinks less
Sweat is cooler when the body is hotter
items.why: Sweating cools the body but loses water. If a camel lets her body warm up, she needs less sweating, so she saves water.

items.p: A giraffe stretches her neck all her life. Will her calf have a longer neck because of that?
opts: No, a calf inherits only the differences she is born with
Yes, stretching passes on to the calf
Yes, but only a little
items.why: What an animal does in her life does not change what she passes on. Giraffe necks became long because longer-necked giraffes in each generation reached more food and had more young.

items.p: In warm water, an octopus's blue blood carries more oxygen than red blood does.
items.why: False. The copper-based blue blood works well in cold water with little oxygen, but it carries less oxygen than red blood in warm water. This is one of the prices of being an octopus.

items.p: Octopuses and humans both have lens eyes because they share a recent ancestor with such an eye.
items.why: False. Our last common ancestor lived over 500 million years ago, and had no lens eye. The two kinds of eyes grew separately, which is called convergent evolution.

items.p: A woodpecker has two toes pointing forward and two toes pointing ____.
items.why: This grip is called zygodactyl. It lets her cling to a straight trunk, with her stiff tail pressed against it.

items.p: Match each pair of animals to the problem they both solved, in different ways.
pairs: Catching insects with a long sticky tongue
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each pair met the same problem. They are not close relatives, so each pair found its own answer, with a different body to start from.

items.p: Sort each fact into a gain or a price.
items: A camel floats over soft sand
A camel slips on wet clay
An octopus squeezes into a crack
An octopus tires when she swims
A woodpecker needs trees with wood
items.a: as given
items.why: Every body part has both. The gain is what the part does well. The price is where it fails or what the animal gives up.

items.p: Put the steps of a fair test in order.
a: Ask a question and guess the answer, with a reason
Say what I thought, what I saw and why
items.why: A fair test starts with a question and a guess. Then only one thing changes, so any difference must come from it. The measuring comes last, followed by saying what it means.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? A chisel beak, a stiff tail, a long sticky tongue, a wide soft pad.
items.a: The wide soft pad, because it belongs to a camel. The other three belong to a woodpecker.
items.why: A woodpecker has a chisel beak, a stiff tail and a long sticky tongue. A wide soft pad is a camel's foot.

items.p: A foot 3 centimetres wide sinks 6 millimetres into dough. A foot twice as wide sinks 2 millimetres. How many times as deep is the first dent?
items.why: 6 divided by 2 is 3. The narrow foot sank 3 times as deep. Doubling the width makes the area 4 times as big, so the push on each patch is 4 times smaller, and the dent is much shallower.

items.p: Explain why a camel with fat spread all over her body would find desert heat harder than a camel with a hump. Use what you know about insulation.
items.a: Fat is an insulator, and it traps heat. If it covered the whole body, the camel's heat would stay in and she would need to sweat a lot, using up water. In a hump, the fat leaves most of the skin thin, so her body heat can leave.
items.why: A strong answer says that fat is insulation, that insulation holds heat in, and that the hump leaves the rest of the body free to lose heat.

items.p: A visitor at an aquarium says that an octopus is a simple animal, because she has no bones and no shell.

views.says: No bones, no shell and no armour. She looks simple to me.
She has about 500 million nerve cells, three hearts, a lens eye and arms that taste. Soft is not the same as simple.

views.who: A fisher in Kochi (an imagined view)
views.says: I have seen an octopus open a trap and walk out of a basket. She learns fast. I would not call her simple.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most, and why?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer says that having no bones does not make an animal simple, and gives evidence such as the nerve cells, the three hearts or the escapes.
items.why: The biologist and the fisher give evidence. The visitor judges by one missing part. A body without a skeleton is made differently, and not more simply.

items.p: Draw an octopus squeezing into a crack in a rock. Label the one big hard part that sets how small a gap she can pass.
items.a: An octopus with soft arms and body flowing into a crack, and a label pointing to the beak between her arms.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the soft body pouring into the gap, and labels the beak as the hard part that sets the limit.

items.p: Octopuses and humans both have lens eyes, but their eyes grew separately. Why might two kinds of animals end up with the same kind of eye?
items.a: They met the same problem: focusing light to see a sharp picture. A lens is a good answer to that problem, so it appeared twice, from different starting bodies.
items.why: A strong answer names the shared problem, and says that a similar answer can appear twice when the problem is the same.

items.p: A student repeats the Ice Test but gives block C a cloth twice as thick as block B's. C melts less than B. What is wrong with this test?
opts: B and C do not have the same amount of cloth, so the place is no longer the only difference
The ice was too cold
Block A should not be used
items.why: A fair test changes only one thing. If C has more cloth, we cannot tell whether the lump or the amount made the difference.

items.p: A driver lets some air out of a tractor's tyres on soft sand. What is the main effect?
opts: The tyre touches the sand over a bigger patch, so the pressure is smaller
The tractor gets lighter
The sand gets harder
items.why: A softer tyre flattens where it meets the ground, so the same weight is shared over a bigger patch. The tractor has the same weight, and the sand is not changed.

items.p: A study with high-speed video of woodpeckers found that the head acts like a stiff hammer. What idea does this question?
opts: That the skull works mainly as a shock absorber
That woodpeckers hit trees
That woodpeckers have beaks
items.why: The older idea says the skull and tongue bones take up most of the knock. The video study suggests the head passes most of its energy into the wood instead. Scientists are still testing both.

items.p: An animal that needs a new body part will grow it during her lifetime.
items.why: False. Needing a part does not make it appear. Small differences already exist in each generation, and the animals with helpful ones survive and have more young.

items.p: An octopus breathes with ____ inside her mantle.
items.why: Water flows through the mantle and over the gills, where oxygen passes into her blood. The same mantle also gives the jet when she squeezes water out through the funnel.

items.p: Match each body part to its price.
pairs: Uses a lot of energy for hammering
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Every part has a price. A wide pad has no grip on clay. A soft body has nothing hard to protect it. Hammering is hard work. A tall neck means blood must be pushed far up to the head.

items.p: Sort each thing by whether it spreads weight over a big patch or puts it on a small patch.
cats: Spreads weight over a big patch
Puts weight on a small patch
items: Spreads weight over a big patch
Spreads weight over a big patch
Spreads weight over a big patch
Puts weight on a small patch
Puts weight on a small patch
Puts weight on a small patch
items.a: as given
items.why: Wide things share a weight over many small patches, so each is pushed a little. Pointed things push hard on one tiny patch.

items.p: A camel weighs 600 kilograms. She can lose a quarter of her weight in water. How many kilograms of water is that, and how much does she weigh then?
items.a: 150 kilograms lost, 450 kilograms left
items.why: A quarter of 600 is 600 divided by 4, which is 150. 600 take away 150 is 450. She can lose this much water and live. A person is in danger long before losing a quarter of their weight.

items.p: In a test, block A melted to 1.6 centimetres of water in the glass and block B melted to 0.8 centimetres. How many times as much did A melt as B?
items.why: 1.6 divided by 0.8 is 2. Block A melted twice as much as block B.

items.p: Which pair is the odd one out, and why? A bird's wing and a bat's wing, an octopus eye and a human eye, a human hand and a chimpanzee hand.
items.a: The human hand and the chimpanzee hand, because the two are alike since they come from a recent shared ancestor. The other pairs grew separately to solve the same problem.
items.why: Humans and chimpanzees share a recent ancestor with a grasping hand, so their hands are alike by inheritance. Birds and bats, and octopuses and humans, are far apart, and their similar parts grew separately.

items.p: Explain how a camel family could end up with wide pads, without any camel trying to grow them.
items.a: In every generation, calves differ a little. Some have wider pads. On sand, they walk farther and find more food, so they live longer and have more calves. Those calves inherit wide pads. After many generations, wide pads are normal.
items.why: A strong answer names the small differences, the survival and having more young, and the inheriting. It does not say that a camel grew pads by trying.

items.p: Pick an animal from your home or street. Name two of her body parts, the problem each solves and a price for each.
items.a: A house crow has a strong all-purpose beak that eats many foods, and the price is that she is not the best at any one food. Her feet grip railings, and the price is that she walks with a clumsy hop.
items.why: A strong answer names real parts, real problems and honest prices. Any animal you can watch will do.

items.p: A friend's ice test shows the fully wrapped block melting least. She says, 'This proves that fat all over is always better.' Use claim, evidence and reasoning to reply.
items.a: Claim: not always. Evidence: wrapped ice melted least, but that was a model with a cold block in a warm room. Reasoning: a coat is good when you want to keep heat in or out. A camel in the desert wants heat to get out of her body, so fat all over could be a problem.
items.why: A strong answer separates what the test showed from what it did not. It also says that a good part in one place may be a poor part in another.

items.p: A cousin says it would be wonderful to have a camel's body, because camels never need water.

views.says: Camels live in the desert without drinking. I want a body like that.

views.who: A camel keeper in Jaisalmer (an imagined view)
views.says: Camels do need water. A camel loses a lot of weight in water, and then drinks about a hundred litres in minutes. She saves water, she does not do without.
A camel's body has prices too. Her temperature rises a lot, her pads slip on wet ground, and she needs the dry air and cool nights to make it work.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most, and why?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer says that a camel saves water but still needs it, and that her body works well in one kind of place.
items.why: The keeper and the vet say what the evidence shows. The camel's tricks are real, but they save water and do not remove the need for it.

items.p: Draw an octopus using her jet. Show the water going out backwards and the octopus going forward. Add arrows.
items.a: An octopus with a funnel pointing backwards, an arrow for the water going back and an arrow for the octopus going forward.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the jet going one way and the octopus moving the other way. The water is pushed back, and it pushes her forward.

quiz.p: A bird has a very long, thin, curved beak. What should you ask first?
opts: What problem does this beak solve?
How old is the bird?
What is her favourite colour?
quiz.why: An odd part is an answer to a problem in the animal's way of living. Asking about the problem leads you to the food, the place and the price.

quiz.p: A camel keeps her fat in one hump, not all over her body. What is the best reason?
opts: The rest of her skin stays thin, so her body heat can leave
Fat is too heavy to spread out
Fat only grows on the back
quiz.why: Fat is insulation. A layer all over would trap her heat, and she would have to sweat more and lose water.

quiz.p: A thin, hungry camel's hump flops to one side. What does this tell you?
opts: Her body has been using up the fat in it
The hump was full of water and it leaked
She has grown a new hump
quiz.why: The hump is a store of fat. When food is scarce, her body uses it up and the hump shrinks and flops. It is not a tank of water.

quiz.p: The same weight stands on a narrow foot and on a wide foot on soft dough. Which sinks deeper, and why?
opts: The narrow foot, because the same weight is on a smaller patch
The wide foot, because it is bigger
Both sink the same, because the weight is the same
quiz.why: Pressure is weight divided by area. The narrow foot puts all the weight on a smaller area, so each small patch is pushed harder.

quiz.p: A camel's wide foot floats on sand. What is a likely price?
opts: It slips on wet clay
It makes her too light
It stops her from running
quiz.why: A wide pad shares her weight on soft ground, but on slippery clay it has little grip. Every good part is good for one kind of place.

quiz.p: Why do most woodpeckers have two toes pointing backwards?
opts: To grip a straight trunk
To swim
To scratch the ground for seeds
quiz.why: Two toes forward and two back make a strong clamp on a trunk. Her stiff tail props her at the same time.

quiz.p: What do scientists agree on about how a woodpecker's head survives the hits?
opts: They are still testing whether the skull absorbs the shock or acts like a stiff hammer
It is settled that the head has a built-in cushion
It is settled that her brain is never hurt
quiz.why: Older books said she has a shock absorber, but a video study in 2022 found the head works more like a stiff hammer. The question is still open, and we can say so.

quiz.p: How does an octopus move away fast from danger?
opts: She squirts water out of her funnel and shoots the other way
She flaps her wings
She runs on her bones
quiz.why: The water jets backwards, and the push on the water pushes her forward. It works fast but tires her, because the heart that feeds her body slows down.

quiz.p: Why can an octopus squeeze through a gap about as wide as her beak?
opts: She has no bones, so only her beak is hard
She is made of water
She can shrink her beak
quiz.why: The beak is the one big hard part. The rest of her body is soft and flows through any gap that the beak can pass.

quiz.p: Which of these is evidence, not a claim, about the Ice Test?
opts: Block B had the least water in the glass
Fat all over is always best
Insulation traps heat
quiz.why: Evidence is what you measured or saw. A claim says what you think is true. Reasoning explains why the evidence supports the claim.

quiz.p: Which is the best explanation of how camels came to have wide pads?
opts: Calves born with wider pads survived better on sand and left more calves
Camels stretched their feet to fit the sand
Camels wanted wider feet
quiz.why: Wanting or stretching does not change what an animal passes on. Helpful differences spread because those animals survive and have more young.

quiz.p: Octopus eyes and human eyes both have lenses, yet the animals are not close relatives. What best explains this?
opts: Both met the same problem, focusing light, and each found its own answer
An octopus is a kind of human
They share a recent ancestor with lens eyes
quiz.why: This is convergent evolution. A lens is a good answer to the problem of seeing a sharp image, so it appeared twice, from different bodies.

maths.problem: A square foot that is 1 centimetre wide has an area of 1 square centimetre. Feet 2, 3 and 4 centimetres wide have areas of 4, 9 and 16 square centimetres. What is the area of a foot 5 centimetres wide, and what pattern did you use?
maths.answer: 25 square centimetres. The areas are square numbers: 1 times 1, 2 times 2, 3 times 3, 4 times 4, so 5 times 5.
maths.explain: Each area is the width times itself. 5 times 5 is 25. A foot 5 times as wide has 25 times the area, so the same weight gives a push that is 25 times smaller on each patch.
maths.context: In the Foot Test, wider feet had much bigger areas than their widths suggest.
maths.why_maths: Spotting the pattern shows how fast a wider foot spreads a weight, which is why camels and snowshoes work.

maths.problem: In the Foot Test, the narrow foot made dents of 6 millimetres and 8 millimetres in two tries. What is the average dent?
maths.explain: 6 plus 8 is 14. 14 divided by 2 is 7. The average is 7 millimetres.
maths.context: In the Foot Test, you tried each foot twice and took the average.
maths.why_maths: One try can be a fluke. An average of two tries is a fairer number to compare.

maths.problem: Fat holds about twice as much energy as the same weight of sugar. A big camel's hump holds about 30 kilograms of fat. How many kilograms of sugar would hold the same energy?
maths.explain: Fat holds twice the energy of sugar, so you need twice the weight of sugar. 30 times 2 is 60 kilograms. This is why a store of fat is so light for the energy it holds.
maths.context: A camel carries her food store in her hump.
maths.why_maths: Comparing weights shows why an animal that must carry its food chooses fat over sugar.

maths.problem: A person drinks about 2 litres of water a day. A very thirsty camel can drink about 100 litres in a few minutes. How many days of a person's drinking is that?
maths.explain: 100 divided by 2 is 50. A thirsty camel can drink in a few minutes what a person drinks in about seven weeks.
maths.context: A camel can lose a quarter of her weight in water and then drink it all back at once.
maths.why_maths: Dividing shows how big a camel's single drink is, compared to ours.

maths.problem: An octopus has about 500 million nerve cells, and about two thirds of them are in her arms. About how many nerve cells are in her arms?
maths.explain: 500 million divided by 3 is about 167 million, which is one third. Two thirds is 2 times 167 million, which is about 333 million. So most of her nerve cells are in her arms.
maths.context: An octopus has most of her nerve cells in her arms, not in her head.
maths.why_maths: Finding a fraction of a number shows how much of her nervous system lies outside her main brain.

maths.problem: A woodpecker hits the wood 15 times a second in a burst that lasts 6 seconds. She does 10 bursts while she looks for food. How many hits is that in all?
maths.explain: 15 times 6 is 90 hits in one burst. 90 times 10 is 900 hits. A woodpecker's head takes hundreds of hard knocks each time she feeds.
maths.context: A woodpecker's head takes hard knocks every time she feeds.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying shows how many knocks add up, which is why scientists wonder how her head survives.

maths.problem: In an ice test, block A (no cloth) melts to 1.6 centimetres of water, block B (cloth all around) to 0.8 centimetres and block C (the same cloth lumped on top) to 1.4 centimetres. Is block C closer to A or to B? Use the differences to decide.
maths.answer: Closer to A. C is 0.2 centimetres from A and 0.6 centimetres from B.
maths.explain: A minus C is 1.6 minus 1.4, which is 0.2. C minus B is 1.4 minus 0.8, which is 0.6. C is much closer to the bare block, so the lump on top helped little.
maths.context: In the Ice Test, block C had the same cloth as block B, but in a lump on top.
maths.why_maths: Comparing differences turns three numbers into a clear picture of which block is closer to which.

applications: Wide, low-pressure tyres and let-down tyres help vehicles cross desert sand and soft mud.
Snowshoes and wide skis spread a person's weight on snow, in the same way as a camel's pad.
Engineers study octopus arms to build soft robots that can grip odd shapes and enter small gaps.
Engineers study woodpecker heads for ideas for protective packaging and helmets, though how the head works is still debated.
In hot cities, roofs are coated white or insulated, because the roof is where the Sun hits a building.
Doctors and nurses use ideas about pressure when they place people in beds, so that the weight is shared over a bigger area.
Kharai camels of Kutch swim out to islands to eat mangrove leaves, so the camel body can suit a sea coast as well as a desert.
Designers think in trade-offs: a coat, a shoe or a tyre that is better in one place is worse in another.
Farmers use wide-wheeled carts and tractors in soft fields, to avoid sinking.
Cuttlefish and octopus camouflage give ideas for materials that change colour.

open_questions.q: How does a woodpecker's head survive thousands of knocks a day?
open_questions.why_open: Studies disagree about how much the skull and the tongue bones soak up the shock. High-speed video is new, and tests on living woodpeckers are hard to do.

open_questions.q: How does an octopus match the colour of her background when her eyes seem to see no colour?
open_questions.why_open: Some scientists think her skin senses light. Others think the shape of her pupil lets her work out colour. Neither idea has been proved.

open_questions.q: How much does each octopus arm decide for herself?
open_questions.why_open: Most of her nerve cells are in her arms, but nobody knows how orders pass between the arms and the brain, or what, if anything, an arm feels.

open_questions.q: Why do most octopuses live only one to a few years?
open_questions.why_open: Many octopuses die soon after breeding, and a mother often dies as her eggs hatch. Scientists have found a gland that triggers this, but they do not know why evolution kept it.

open_questions.q: How exactly does a camel's kidney make such thick wee, and how does the body avoid damage when very thirsty?
open_questions.why_open: The basic idea is known, but many details of the cells involved are still being studied.

open_questions.q: Could a robot with a soft body work as well as an octopus?
open_questions.why_open: Engineers have made soft robot arms, but none matches the control that an octopus has over eight arms.
